question.text:
Find the inverse of the given Matrix, using Cayley-Hamilton's Theorem.

$$
A=\left[\begin{array}{lll}
4 & 3 & 1 \\
-1 & 2 & 1 \\
3 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right]
$$

  1. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{16}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 & -6 \\ -6 & 9 & 11\end{array}\right]$
     
  2. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{8}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 & -3 \\ -6 & 9 & 11\end{array}\right]$
     
  3. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{16}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -1 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 & -6 \\ -6 & 9 & 11\end{array}\right]$
     
  4. $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{8}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 & -6 \\ -6 & 9 & 11\end{array}\right]$
question.subject: Linear Algebra

question.text:
Suppose $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix so that

$$
A\left[\begin{array}{l}
1 \\
4 \\
2
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}
1 \\
0 \\
0
\end{array}\right], \quad A\left[\begin{array}{l}
3 \\
1 \\
0
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
1 \\
0
\end{array}\right], \text { and } \quad A\left[\begin{array}{l}
2 \\
1 \\
7
\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
0 \\
1
\end{array}\right]
$$


What is the first column of $A^{-1}$ ?

  1. $\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$
     
  2. $\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$
     
  3. $\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$
     
  4. $\left[\begin{array}{l}2 \\ 1 \\ 7\end{array}\right]$
question.subject: Linear Algebra

question.text:
What is the maximum possible rank of an $\mathrm{m} \times \mathrm{n}$ matrix A that is not square?

  1. $\operatorname{rank}(A) \geq \min (m, n)$
  2. $\operatorname{rank}(A) \leq \min (m, n)$
  3. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=\min (m, n)$
  4. $\operatorname{rank}(A)=\max (m, n)$
question.subject: Linear Algebra

question.text:
Let A be an $\mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{n}$ matrix, and A is invertible. Then which of the following statement is equivalent:

  1.  Ax $=0$ has only the trivial solution.
  2. A cannot be expressed as a product of elementary matrices.
  3. $\mathrm{Ax}=\mathrm{b}$ is inconsistent for every $\mathrm{n} \times 1$ matrix b .
  4. $\mathrm{Ax}=\mathrm{b}$ has more than one solution for every $\mathrm{n} \times 1$ matrix b
question.subject: Linear Algebra

question.text:
The eigenvalues of the matrix $A=\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{array}\right]$ are:

  1. 1 and 0
  2. 1 and 6
  3. 2 and 3
  4. 0 and 7
question.subject: Linear Algebra
